title: What Are All the Rules and Principles of Cricket?
content:
WHAT ARE ALL THE RULES AND PRINCIPLES OF CRICKET?

Cricket is a bat-and-ball sport played between two teams. The official Laws of Cricket are maintained by the Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC). The Laws contain 42 main Laws covering players, umpires, the ball, bat, pitch, wickets, scoring, dismissals, fair play and player conduct. Different formats and competitions can also have additional playing conditions.

LAW 1 — THE PLAYERS
A cricket team normally consists of 11 players. One player is the captain. Only the permitted number of players can participate on the field according to the Laws and playing conditions.

LAW 2 — THE UMPIRES
Umpires control the match and make decisions according to the Laws. They decide matters such as wickets, boundaries, no-balls, wides, dead balls and other incidents.

LAW 3 — THE SCORERS
Scorers record runs, wickets, overs and other important match information. They work with the umpires to maintain an accurate score.

LAW 4 — THE BALL
The cricket ball must meet the specifications required by the Laws. The condition and replacement of the ball are controlled according to the Laws and applicable playing conditions.

LAW 5 — THE BAT
The bat must comply with the required size, materials and construction rules. The batter uses the bat to play the ball and score runs.

LAW 6 — THE PITCH
The pitch is the central area between the two wickets. It has specified dimensions and is prepared and maintained for the match.

LAW 7 — THE CREASES
The bowling, popping and return creases mark important areas of the pitch. They help determine the positions of the batter, bowler and fielders and whether a batter is within their ground.

LAW 8 — THE WICKETS
There are two wickets on the pitch. Each wicket consists of three stumps with two bails on top. A wicket can be broken in the ways defined by the Laws.

LAW 9 — PREPARATION AND MAINTENANCE OF THE PLAYING AREA
The playing area and pitch must be prepared and maintained according to the Laws. Ground conditions must be managed so that play can take place properly.

LAW 10 — COVERING THE PITCH
The pitch may be covered according to the Laws and playing conditions. Covers are commonly used to protect the pitch from rain and weather.

LAW 11 — INTERVALS
Matches contain scheduled intervals. These can include intervals between innings and other intervals specified by the Laws or playing conditions.

LAW 12 — START OF PLAY; CESSATION OF PLAY
The umpires determine when play starts, stops and resumes. Weather, bad light, interruptions and other circumstances can affect play.

LAW 13 — INNINGS
An innings is the period during which a team or batter has the opportunity to score runs. The number and length of innings depend on the match format and playing conditions.

LAW 14 — THE FOLLOW-ON
In certain multi-innings matches, the team batting second may be required to bat again immediately if it has scored sufficiently fewer runs than the team batting first. The exact conditions depend on the Laws and playing conditions.

LAW 15 — DECLARATION AND FORFEITURE
In a multi-innings match, a captain may declare an innings closed before all wickets have fallen. An innings may also be forfeited according to the Laws.

LAW 16 — THE RESULT
A match may result in a win, loss, tie, draw or another result according to the format and applicable playing conditions.

LAW 17 — THE OVER
An over consists of six valid balls. No-balls and wides do not count as one of the six valid balls of an over.

LAW 18 — SCORING RUNS
Runs can be scored by running between the wickets, hitting boundaries and through extras. Runs are added to the team's total according to the Laws.

LAW 19 — BOUNDARIES
A boundary occurs when the ball reaches or crosses the boundary according to the Laws. A normal boundary four is scored when the ball reaches the boundary after touching the ground. A six is normally scored when the ball is struck over the boundary without touching the ground.

LAW 20 — DEAD BALL
The ball becomes dead when circumstances specified by the Laws occur. Once the ball is dead, play from that delivery has ended until the ball is put back into play.

LAW 21 — NO BALL
A no-ball is called when the bowler delivers the ball illegally under the Laws. A no-ball gives the batting side an extra run and does not count as a valid ball of the over. Additional runs may also be scored from the delivery.

LAW 22 — WIDE BALL
A wide is called when a delivery is too far from the batter to be reasonably hit, subject to the Laws and playing conditions. A wide gives the batting side an extra run and does not count as a valid ball of the over.

LAW 23 — BYE AND LEG BYE
A bye is a run scored when the ball passes the batter without touching the bat or person. A leg bye is scored when the ball touches the batter's person under the conditions permitted by the Laws.

LAW 24 — FIELDER'S ABSENCE; SUBSTITUTES
The Laws explain what happens when a fielder is absent and when a substitute fielder can be used. Restrictions apply to substitute fielders.

LAW 25 — BATTER'S INNINGS; RUNNERS
This Law deals with the batter's innings and runners. The use of runners is subject to the Laws and applicable playing conditions.

LAW 26 — PRACTICE ON THE FIELD
Practice activities on the field are restricted. Players must follow the Laws and must not unfairly delay or interfere with play.

LAW 27 — THE WICKET-KEEPER
The wicket-keeper is the designated fielder behind the striker's wicket. The wicket-keeper has specific responsibilities and restrictions under the Laws.

LAW 28 — THE FIELDER
Fielders must follow the Laws regarding their positions and actions. They must not unfairly distract, deceive or obstruct the batter.

LAW 29 — THE WICKET IS BROKEN
The Laws define when a wicket is broken. Normally a bail must be completely removed from the stumps or a stump must be removed from the ground in the circumstances specified by the Laws.

LAW 30 — BATTER OUT OF THEIR GROUND
A batter is out of their ground when neither the bat nor part of their person is grounded behind the relevant popping crease. This is important for run outs and stumpings.

LAW 31 — APPEALS
An umpire generally cannot give a batter out unless the fielding side appeals, subject to the Laws. An appeal asks the umpire to make a decision about a possible dismissal.

LAW 32 — BOWLED
A batter is out Bowled when a legal delivery breaks the striker's wicket, subject to the conditions of the Law.

LAW 33 — CAUGHT
A batter is out Caught when a fielder legally catches the ball after it has touched the batter's bat, subject to the conditions of the Law, before the ball touches the ground.

LAW 34 — HIT THE BALL TWICE
A batter can be out for deliberately hitting the ball twice, except where a second contact is permitted by the Law, such as protecting the wicket in certain circumstances.

LAW 35 — HIT WICKET
A batter is out Hit Wicket when their wicket is broken by their bat or person in the circumstances specified by the Law.

LAW 36 — LEG BEFORE WICKET
LBW is a method of dismissal. The umpire considers where the ball pitched, where it struck the batter, whether it would have hit the wicket and the other conditions required by the Law.

LAW 37 — OBSTRUCTING THE FIELD
A batter can be out for deliberately obstructing or distracting the fielding side by word or action, subject to the conditions and exceptions in the Law.

LAW 38 — RUN OUT
A batter is Run Out when, while the ball is in play, their wicket is fairly broken while they are out of their ground, subject to the conditions of the Law.

LAW 39 — STUMPED
A batter is Stumped when the wicket-keeper fairly breaks the wicket while the batter is out of their ground and is not attempting a run, subject to the conditions of the Law.

LAW 40 — TIMED OUT
A new batter must be ready within the time specified by the Laws and applicable playing conditions. Failure to meet the requirement can result in a Timed Out dismissal.

LAW 41 — UNFAIR PLAY
The Laws prohibit unfair actions, including certain forms of deliberate distraction, unfair movement, illegal interference with the ball, damaging the pitch and other actions that give an unfair advantage.

LAW 42 — PLAYERS' CONDUCT
Players must behave properly and respect opponents, umpires and the Spirit of Cricket. The Law defines levels of misconduct and the actions that umpires can take.

MAIN DISMISSALS IN CRICKET
The main methods of dismissal are Bowled, Caught, LBW, Run Out, Stumped, Hit Wicket, Hit the Ball Twice, Obstructing the Field and Timed Out. Each dismissal has its own conditions.

EXTRAS IN CRICKET
The main extras are no-balls, wides, byes and leg byes. Extras contribute to the team's total but are treated differently in the batter's individual score.

BASIC CRICKET PRINCIPLES
The basic principles of cricket include fair play, following the Laws, respecting umpires and opponents, protecting the spirit of the game, scoring runs, taking wickets and playing within the conditions of the competition.

CRICKET FORMATS
Test cricket, ODI cricket and T20 cricket have different match structures and playing conditions. Test matches are multi-day matches, ODIs are limited-overs matches and T20 matches are shorter limited-overs matches. Exact rules such as over limits, fielding restrictions, reviews and other regulations can vary according to the current competition playing conditions.

SPIRIT OF CRICKET
Cricket is based not only on competition but also on fairness, respect, discipline and sportsmanship. Players are expected to respect the umpires, opponents and the game.

IMPORTANT NOTE
The official Laws of Cricket are maintained by the Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC). ICC and individual competitions publish additional playing conditions for particular formats and tournaments. Therefore, the exact rules used in a particular match should always be checked against the latest official MCC Laws and the relevant competition playing conditions.
